Global Well-posedness of a System of Nonlinearly Coupled KdV equations of Majda and Biello

Date: September 27, 2013
Abstract.

This paper addresses the problem of global well-posedness of a coupled system of Korteweg-de Vries equations, derived by Majda and Biello in the context of nonlinear resonant interaction of Rossby waves, in a periodic setting in homogeneous Sobolev spaces H˙s\dot{H}^{s}, for s≥0s\geq 0. Our approach is based on a successive time-averaging method developed by Babin, Ilyin and Titi [1].

Key words and phrases: 
KdV equation, global well-posedness, successive time-averaging method
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B34,35Q53

1. Introduction

The present manuscript is motivated by a work of Babin, Ilyin and Titi [1] explaining the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. In [1] the authors exploit the dispersive structure which introduces frequency dependent fast oscillations by means of successive integrations by parts and time averaging. Our aim is to adapt this method in order to obtain analogous well-posedness results for certain system of coupled Korteweg-de Vries equations (cKdV):

{At=α​Ax​x​x−(A​B)xBt=Bx​x​x−A​Ax\begin{cases}A_{t}=\alpha A_{xxx}-(AB)_{x}\\ B_{t}=B_{xxx}-AA_{x}\\ \end{cases} (1.1)

introduced by Majda and Biello (see [2, 3, 4, 13] and references therein). This system arises in the study of nonlinear resonant interactions of equatorial baroclinic and barotropic Rossby waves, and is a model for long range interactions between the tropical and midlatitude troposphere. In (1.1), AA is the amplitude of an equatorially confined (baroclinic) Rossby wave packet, and BB is the amplitude of a (barotropic) Rossby wave packet with significant energy in the midlatitudes, and α\alpha is a parameter close to 11.

Several conservation laws are known for (1.1):

E1:=∫A​𝑑x,E2:=∫B​𝑑xE_{1}:=\int A\>\mathrm{d}x\>,\quad E_{2}:=\int B\>\mathrm{d}x (1.2)

and most important for our purpose, the total energy

E:=∫A2+B2​𝑑x,E:=\int A^{2}+B^{2}\>\mathrm{d}x\>,

which bounds the L2L^{2}-norm. In addition, as elaborated in [4], system (1.1), enjoys a Hamiltonian structure, where the Hamiltonian is given by

H:=12​∫α​Ax2+Bx2+A2​B​𝑑x.H:=\frac{1}{2}\int\alpha A_{x}^{2}+B_{x}^{2}+A^{2}B\>\mathrm{d}x\>.

In contrast to the 1-d KdV no more conservation laws are known for (1.1), so it is not necessarily completely integrable. However, to show the global well-posedness of weak solutions of (1.1), with initial data in L2L^{2}, we only use the conservation of the total energy and in particular we will not take advantage of the conservation of the Hamiltonian.

In [2], Biello used the change of variables U=12​(2​B+A)U=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sqrt{2}B+A) and V=12​(2​B−A)V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sqrt{2}B-A) to transform (1.1) into an idealized “symmetric” model (when α=1\alpha=1)

{Ut=Ux​x​x−U​Ux+12​(U​V)xVt=Vx​x​x−V​Vx+12​(U​V)x\begin{cases}U_{t}=U_{xxx}-UU_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(UV)_{x}\\ V_{t}=V_{xxx}-VV_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(UV)_{x}\end{cases} (1.3)

and studied its soliton solutions. In this paper, we will consider system (1.3) subject to periodic boundary conditions, with basic periodic domain 𝕋=[0,2​π]\mathbb{T}=[0,2\pi]; which is equivalent to consider (1.3) on the unit circle. Note that there are two invariant subspaces, U=0U=0 or V=0V=0. In case of U=0U=0 the solution for VV evolves according to a standard KdV (respectively UU if V=0V=0 is taken).

Since system (1.3) is closely connected to the KdV equation ut=ux​x​x+u​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}+uu_{x}, we now briefly review some important results concerning the KdV, with periodic boundary condition. In his seminal papers [5, 6] Bourgain introduced a new type of weighted Sobolev spaces Xs,b​(ℝ×𝕋)X^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T}) for functions in time and space, the so-called dispersive Sobolev spaces, which is the closure of the Schwartz space under the norm

‖u‖Xs,b​(ℝ×𝕋)=‖⟨k⟩s​⟨τ+k3⟩b​u^​(τ,k)‖Lτ2​lk2​(ℝ×ℤ),\left\|u\right\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T})}=\left\|\langle k\rangle^{s}\langle\tau+k^{3}\rangle^{b}\widehat{u}(\tau,k)\right\|_{L_{\tau}^{2}l_{k}^{2}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z})}\>, (1.4)

where ⟨⋅⟩=(1+|⋅|2)1/2\langle\cdot\rangle=(1+|\cdot|^{2})^{1/2} and u^\widehat{u} denotes the Fourier transform in space and time. These spaces reflect the fact that the Fourier transform of a solution of the unperturbed (dispersive) part of the KdV is supported on the characteristic hyperplane τ+k3=0\tau+k^{3}=0 described by its dispersion relation. In fact, the Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces are an efficient tool to capture the phenomenon that the solutions to KdV, after localisation in time, have space-time Fourier transform supported near the characteristic surface; thus the nonlinearity does not significantly alter the space-time Fourier “path” of the solution, at least for short time (see [17]). The definition can of course be adapted to account for other dispersive PDEs like Schrödinger equation. Using this Bourgain proved local well-posedness the KdV in L2​(𝕋)L^{2}(\mathbb{T}) by means of Banach’s Fixed Point principle. This result was improved by Kenig, Ponce and Vega [11]. They proved a sharp bilinear estimate for the norm in (1.4) and showed local well-posedness in H−1/2(𝕋)H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{T}). The corresponding global well-posedness result in H−1/2(𝕋)H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{T}) has been proved by Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka and Tao [7] by employing the II-method (or the method of almost conserved quantities); here, “II” stands for a mollification operator, acting like the Identity on low frequencies, and like an Integration operator on high frequencies. Kappeler and Topalov [12] were able to prove global well-posedness in H−1​(𝕋)H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}) by using the complete integrability of the KdV.

The Majda-Biello system (1.1) is a member of a wider class of KdV-type systems. Another model among several other systems of this class is for example the Gear-Grimshaw system [8]. In [14] Oh investigated system (1.1) by employing Xs,bX^{s,b}-estimates and obtained local well-posedness results depending on the value of the parameter α\alpha. For α=1\alpha=1 he obtained local well-posedness in (a cross-product of) H−1/2(𝕋)H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{T}) and he proved local well-posedness for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}), s>1/2s>1/2. The reason for this is that if α≠0\alpha\not=0 certain nontrivial resonances occur (which can be described by using diophantine conditions) because the space-time Fourier transforms of solutions of the two linear parts of the system are supported on different hyperplanes described by their dispersion relation. Corresponding global well-posedness results have also been proved by Oh [15] using the II-method. If α=1\alpha=1 system (1.1) is globally well-posed in H−1/2(𝕋)H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{T}); while for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) it is globally well-posed in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}), s>5/7s>5/7.

In this paper we use the technique of successive differentiation by parts introduced by Babin, Ilyin and Titi [1] on system (1.3) with periodic boundary condition. The first step of the method is to apply the transform

Uk​(t)=e−i​k3​t​uk​(t),Vk​(t)=e−i​k3​t​vk​(t),k∈ℤ,U_{k}(t)=e^{-ik^{3}t}u_{k}(t)\>,\;V_{k}(t)=e^{-ik^{3}t}v_{k}(t)\>,\;k\in\mathbb{Z}, (1.5)

on the Fourier coefficients. This transform represents the action of the unitary group generated by the third derivative, Ψ⁡(t)=e∂x3t\Psi(t)=e^{\partial_{x}^{3}t}, on each Fourier coefficient. In the terminology of quantum mechanics transform (1.5) means the transition to the so-called interaction representation [9]. This can be interpreted in terms of the spaces Xs,bX^{s,b}: a function uu of space and time is in Xs,bX^{s,b} if and only if its interaction representation Ψ⁡(−t)​u​(t)\Psi(-t)u(t) is in the mixed Sobolev space Htb​HxsH_{t}^{b}H_{x}^{s}. The transform (1.5) generates a fast rotation term into the equation, and then several forms of the system are derived using successive differentiations by parts in time (which correspond to integrations by parts in time) after resonances are singled out. The equation becomes of higher algebraic order but we can take advantage of smoothing properties of the higher order operators involved which allows less regular solutions. In principle, this is similar to the idea of normal forms by Shatah [16]. After establishing the global existence in the homogeneous Sobolev space H˙s\dot{H}^{s} for s>0s>0 by using Galerkin method, we prove uniqueness of solutions by means of the Banach’s Fixed Point Theorem. In [1], for constructing a strict contraction mapping, the authors inverted a linear operator that involves the initial value. The inversion and a time-independent estimate on its inverse were done by finding an explicit solution to a boundary value problem for an ODE. However, for the Majda-Biello cKdV system, we run into the difficulty of now having to solve a system of 1D boundary-value problem explicitly. For the sake of bypassing this obstacle, we use a proper splitting of solutions based on high and low Fourier modes, and recast the differentiation by parts procedures to terms involving high frequencies. This idea avoids treating the invertibility of a linear operator, and simply takes advantage of the time-averaging induced squeezing. Such strategy was first introduced in [1] to deal with the less regular initial data in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2]. The authors of [10] followed the idea from [1] to obtain unconditional well-posedness of modified KdV in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for s≥1/2s\geq 1/2. Finally, we must stress that, the present work does not aim to improve the results in [14, 15]; but, our purpose is to provide another example of employing the techniques in [1] which is general enough to apply to other nonlinear dispersive and wave equations for establishing global well-posedness. Although the Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces are a powerful tool to study dispersive equations, in this paper, we simply use the standard Sobolev spaces HsH^{s} in a systematic and natural manner.

This paper is organized as follows. In Sections 2, 3 and 4 we derive several forms of the cKdV (1.3) analogously to [1]. In Section 5 we prove global existence of a solution in the homogeneous Sobolev space H˙s\dot{H}^{s}, for s>0s>0, using a Galerkin scheme and we establish uniform bounds for the solution on each finite time interval. Section 6 is dedicated to regular initial data, that is s>1/2s>1/2, where uniqueness is obtained by means of Banach’s Contraction Principle. Section 7 addresses less regular initial data, i.e., s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2]. For the sake of convenience we use similar notations as in [1] due to the fact that most of the nonlinear operators occurring in this work have the same mapping properties as the ones proven there. Therefore, throughout this work, most relevant estimates of nonlinear operators will be taken from the appendix section and their proofs can be found in [1].

2. Transformations of the system and main results

In this section, we write the cKdV (1.3) in terms of Fourier coefficients, and use a transform of variables in order to introduce oscillating exponentials into the nonlinear term. Based on the transformed system, we shall define a notion of (weak) solutions and state the main results of the present paper.

As mentioned in the Introduction, we consider the Majda-Biello system

{Ut=Ux​x​x−U​Ux+12​(U​V)xVt=Vx​x​x−V​Vx+12​(U​V)xU⁡(0,x)=Uin​(x),V⁡(0,x)=Vin​(x)\begin{cases}U_{t}=U_{xxx}-UU_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(UV)_{x}\\ V_{t}=V_{xxx}-VV_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(UV)_{x}\\ U(0,x)=U^{\text{in}}(x)\>,\;V(0,x)=V^{\text{in}}(x)\end{cases} (2.1)

where x∈𝕋=[0,2​π]x\in\mathbb{T}=[0,2\pi], with periodic boundary condition U⁡(t,0)=U⁡(t,2​π)U(t,0)=U(t,2\pi) (the same for VV). Here, UU and VV are real-valued functions. If (U,V)(U,V) is a smooth solution of (2.1) we observe, from (1.2), the conservation of the mean values, i.e.,

dd​t​∫02​πU⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=dd​t​∫02​πV⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=0.\frac{d}{dt}\int_{0}^{2\pi}U(t,x)dx=\frac{d}{dt}\int_{0}^{2\pi}V(t,x)dx=0.

We assume from now that the initial data and the solution both have spatial mean value zero.

Denote ℤ0:=ℤ\{0}\mathbb{Z}_{0}:=\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0\}. We make a Fourier expansion for UU

U⁡(t,x)=∑k∈ℤ0Uk​(t)​ei​k​x,Uk∈ℂ,Uk​(t)=12​π​∫02​πU⁡(t,x)​e−i​k​x​𝑑x,k∈ℤ0,U(t,x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}}U_{k}(t)e^{ikx}\>,\;U_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\>,\;U_{k}(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}U(t,x)e^{-ikx}\>\mathrm{d}x\>,\quad k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\>, (2.2)

as well as for VV. Furthermore, we observe that U¯k=U−k\overline{U}_{k}=U_{-k}, since we are seeking real valued solutions. Therefore, we denote by H˙s​(𝕋)\dot{H}^{s}(\mathbb{T}) the homogeneous Sobolev spaces of order ss on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, which is a subspace of L1​(𝕋)L^{1}(\mathbb{T}) functions with mean value zero endowed with the norm

‖U‖H˙s2:=∑k∈ℤ0|k|2​s​|Uk|2.\left\|U\right\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}^{2}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}}|k|^{2s}|U_{k}|^{2}\>.

For s=0s=0 this is a normalized version of the L2L^{2}-Norm

‖U‖H˙02=12​π​‖U‖L22.\left\|U\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left\|U\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\>.

Plugging (2.2) into equation (2.1) yields the infinite coupled system

{∂tUk=−i​k3​Uk+12​i​k​∑k1+k2=k(Uk1​Vk2−Uk1​Uk2)∂tVk=−i​k3​Vk+12​i​k​∑k1+k2=k(Uk1​Vk2−Vk1​Vk2)Uk(0)=Ukin,Vk(0)=Vkin,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}U_{k}=-ik^{3}U_{k}+\frac{1}{2}ik\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}\left(U_{k_{1}}V_{k_{2}}-U_{k_{1}}U_{k_{2}}\right)\\ \partial_{t}V_{k}=-ik^{3}V_{k}+\frac{1}{2}ik\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}\left(U_{k_{1}}V_{k_{2}}-V_{k_{1}}V_{k_{2}}\right)\\ U_{k}(0)=U_{k}^{\text{in}}\>,\;V_{k}(0)=V_{k}^{\text{in}}\>,\end{cases} (2.3)

for k∈ℤ0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}. We now apply the transform

Uk​(t)=e−i​k3​t​uk​(t),Vk​(t)=e−i​k3​t​vk​(t),k∈ℤ0,U_{k}(t)=e^{-ik^{3}t}u_{k}(t)\>,\;V_{k}(t)=e^{-ik^{3}t}v_{k}(t)\>,\;k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\>, (2.4)

in order to eliminate the linear terms in (2.3). By means of the identity

(k1+k2)3=3​(k1+k2)​k1​k2+k13+k23(k_{1}+k_{2})^{3}=3(k_{1}+k_{2})k_{1}k_{2}+k_{1}^{3}+k_{2}^{3} (2.5)

equation (2.3) becomes

{∂tuk=12​i​k​∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​t​(uk1​vk2−uk1​uk2)∂tvk=12​i​k​∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​t​(uk1​vk2−vk1​vk2)uk​(0)=ukin,vk​(0)=vkin,k∈ℤ0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u_{k}=\frac{1}{2}ik\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t}\left(u_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}-u_{k_{1}}u_{k_{2}}\right)\\ \partial_{t}v_{k}=\frac{1}{2}ik\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t}\left(u_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}-v_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}\right)\\ u_{k}(0)=u_{k}^{\text{in}}\>,\;v_{k}(0)=v_{k}^{\text{in}}\end{cases},\;\;k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\;. (2.6)

We emphasize that the fast oscillating term e3​i​k​k1​k2​te^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t} in (2.6) reduces the “strength” of the nonlinear term and make it milder, which is the underlying mechanism for prolonging the lifespan of the solutions [1].

Observe that identity (2.5) was also used in the original work of Bourgain [6]. Also notice transform (2.4) is isometric in H˙s\dot{H}^{s}. Using the same notation as in [1], we can write (2.6) as

∂t(ukvk)=(B1​(u,v)k−B1​(u,u)kB1​(u,v)k−B1​(v,v)k),k∈ℤ0,\partial_{t}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{k}\\ v_{k}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B_{1}(u,v)_{k}-B_{1}(u,u)_{k}\\ B_{1}(u,v)_{k}-B_{1}(v,v)_{k}\end{array}\right)\>,\;k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\>, (2.7)

with (u⁡(0),v⁡(0))=(uin,vin)(u(0),v(0))=(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}}), where the bilinear operator B1​(ϕ,ψ)B_{1}(\phi,\psi) is defined by

B1​(ϕ,ψ)k:=12​i​k​∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​t​ϕk1​ψk2.B_{1}(\phi,\psi)_{k}:=\frac{1}{2}ik\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t}\phi_{k_{1}}\psi_{k_{2}}\>. (2.8)

We now define our notion of a (weak) solution of (2.6).

Definition 2.1.

Given the initial data (uin,vin)∈(H˙0)2(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}. We call a function (u,v)(u,v) a solution of (2.6) over the time interval [0,T][0,T] if (u,v)∈L∞​([0,T],(H˙0)2)(u,v)\in L^{\infty}([0,T];(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}) and if the integrated version of (2.6), that is

(uk​(t)vk​(t))−(ukinvkin)=12​i​k​∫0t∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​τ​(uk1​vk2−uk1​uk2uk1​vk2−vk1​vk2)​𝑑τ,\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{k}(t)\\ v_{k}(t)\end{array}\right)-\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{k}^{\text{in}}\\ v_{k}^{\text{in}}\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{2}ik\int_{0}^{t}\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}\tau}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}-u_{k_{1}}u_{k_{2}}\\ u_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}-v_{k_{1}}v_{k_{2}}\end{array}\right)\>\mathrm{d}\tau\>, (2.9)

is satisfied for every k∈ℤ0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}. By means of (2.4) we ultimately get a (weak) solution of the Majda-Biello system (2.1).

Remark 2.2.

It is readily seen from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that

supt∈[0,T]|∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​t​(uk1​(t)​vk2​(t)−uk1​(t)​uk2​(t))|≤‖(u,v)‖L∞​([0,T],(H˙0)2)2.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\left|\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t}(u_{k_{1}}(t)v_{k_{2}}(t)-u_{k_{1}}(t)u_{k_{2}}(t))\right|\leq\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T];(\dot{H}^{0})^{2})}^{2}\>. (2.10)

Therefore, by (2.9), uk​(t)u_{k}(t) is absolutely continuous (for every kk) over the interval [0,T][0,T], which implies uk​(t)u_{k}(t) is differentiable a.e. on [0,T][0,T] (same for vk​(t)v_{k}(t)). Consequently, equation (2.6), the differential form of (2.9), is satisfied for almost every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Also the continuity of uk​(t)u_{k}(t) and vk​(t)v_{k}(t) implies that (u,v)(u,v) is a weak continuous function mapping from [0,T][0,T] to (H˙0)2(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}.

The main result of this manuscript is the global well-posedness for the cKdV (2.6) in the space (H˙s)2(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}, for s≥0s\geq 0. More precisely, we have the following:

Theorem 2.3.

(Global well-posedness) Let s≥0s\geq 0, (u​i​n,v​i​n)∈(H˙s)2(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}, and T>0T>0. Then there exists a unique solution (u⁡(t),v⁡(t))∈C⁡([0,T],(H˙s)2)(u(t),v(t))\in C([0,T];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}) of the cKdV (2.6), in the sense of Definition 2.1, with (u⁡(0),v⁡(0))=(u​i​n,v​i​n)(u(0),v(0))=(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}}), such that

‖(u,v)‖L∞​([0,T],(H˙s)2)≤C⁡(‖(u​i​n,v​i​n)‖(H˙0)2,T,s).\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2})}\leq C\left(\left\|(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}},T,s\right)\>. (2.11)

Moreover, the quantity

ℰ⁡(u⁡(t),v⁡(t)):=2​‖u⁡(t)‖H˙02+2​‖v⁡(t)‖H˙02+‖u⁡(t)−v⁡(t)‖H˙02\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(u(t),v(t)):=2\left\|u(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}+2\left\|v(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}+\left\|u(t)-v(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2} (2.12)

is conserved in time. In addition, the solution depends continuously on the initial data in the sense that

where (u,v)(u,v), (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) are solutions of (2.6) corresponding to the initial data (u​i​n,v​i​n)(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}}), (u~​i​n,v~​i​n)(\tilde{u}^{\emph{in}},\tilde{v}^{\emph{in}}) respectively, and L>0L>0 depends on TT, ss, and max⁡{‖(u​i​n,v​i​n)‖(H˙0)2,‖(u~​i​n,v~​i​n)‖(H˙0)2}\max\left\{\left\|(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}},\left\|(\tilde{u}^{\emph{in}},\tilde{v}^{\emph{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}\right\}.

3. First differentiation by parts in time

As already mentioned above we want to derive different forms of the cKdV (2.6) in order to obtain operators which have better mapping properties than B1B_{1}, given in (2.8), and whose regularity is specified in Lemma 8.1. This will be formally done by the differentiation by parts procedure as described in the sequel. One observes that (2.6) is equivalent to

Remark 3.1.

The mapping properties of B2B_{2} and R3R_{3} are better than those of B1B_{1} (see the Appendix). So the first form (3) is “milder” than the original cKdV (2.6), which is the purpose of the differentiation by parts procedure. On the other hand, we remark that these two forms, (3) and (2.6), are not equivalent. Clearly, any smooth functions that satisfy the original equation (2.6) are also solutions of the newly derived equation (3), but the converse may not be true. Nonetheless, if one is able to show the uniqueness of solutions to (3), then it follows that (2.6) cannot have more than one solution. Hence, in order to prove the uniqueness for (2.6), our strategy is to consider the equation after the first (or the second) differentiation by parts procedure (see Section 6 and 7 for details).

‖𝐁3​(u,v)‖(H˙s+2)2≤C⁡(s)​‖(u,v)‖(H˙s)23, for ​s≥0.\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{B}_{3}(u,v)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s+2})^{2}}\leq C(s)\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3},\text{\;\;for\;\;}s\geq 0. (4.13)

On the other hand, each term in 𝐁4​(u,v)k\mathbf{B}_{4}(u,v)_{k} is either ±i72​B41​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η)\pm\frac{i}{72}B_{4}^{1}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta) or ±i72​B42​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η)\pm\frac{i}{72}B_{4}^{2}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta) with each of the four arguments being uu or vv. Due to Lemma 8.8, the multi-linear operator B4​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η)B_{4}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta) defined by

B4​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η):=B41​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η)+B42​(ϕ,ψ,ξ,η)B_{4}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta):=B_{4}^{1}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta)+B_{4}^{2}(\phi,\psi,\xi,\eta)

has nice smoothing property, which yields

‖𝐁4​(u,v)‖(H˙s+ϵ)2≤C⁡(s,ϵ)​‖(u,v)‖(H˙s)24,\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{B}_{4}(u,v)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s+\epsilon})^{2}}\leq C(s,\epsilon)\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{4}, (4.14)

for s≥0s\geq 0 and ϵ∈(0,12)\epsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{2}).

5. Global existence for s>0s>0

In this section we address the global existence of solutions of the cKdV (2.6). For this purpose we utilize a Galerkin version of equation (2.6) which reads

{∂t(ukNvkN)=12​i​𝒫​k​∑k1+k2=ke3​i​k​k1​k2​t​((𝒫​uk1N)​(𝒫​vk2N)−(𝒫​uk1N)​(𝒫​uk2N)(𝒫​uk1N)​(𝒫​vk2N)−(𝒫​vk1N)​(𝒫​vk2N))uNk(0)=uink,vNk(0)=vink,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{k}^{N}\\ v_{k}^{N}\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{2}i\mathcal{P}k\sum_{k_{1}+k_{2}=k}e^{3ikk_{1}k_{2}t}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}(\mathcal{P}u_{k_{1}}^{N})(\mathcal{P}v_{k_{2}}^{N})-(\mathcal{P}u_{k_{1}}^{N})(\mathcal{P}u_{k_{2}}^{N})\\ (\mathcal{P}u_{k_{1}}^{N})(\mathcal{P}v_{k_{2}}^{N})-(\mathcal{P}v_{k_{1}}^{N})(\mathcal{P}v_{k_{2}}^{N})\end{array}\right)\\ u^{N}_{k}(0)=u^{\text{in}}_{k}\;,\;\;v^{N}_{k}(0)=v^{\text{in}}_{k},\end{cases} (5.1)

for k∈ℤ0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}. Here 𝒫\mathcal{P} denotes the projection on the low Fourier modes |k|≤N|k|\leq N, that is,

𝒫​u=∑|k|≤Nuk​ei​k​x​ and ​𝒫​uk=(𝒫​u)k={ukif|k|≤N0if|k|>N.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}u=\sum_{|k|\leq N}u_{k}e^{ikx}\text{\;\;and\;\;}\mathcal{P}u_{k}=(\mathcal{P}u)_{k}=\Big\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}u_{k}&\text{if}&|k|\leq N\\ 0&\text{if}&|k|>N\end{array}.

We stress that the operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} depends on NN. For the sake of conciseness, we choose the notation 𝒫\mathcal{P} instead of 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N}.

It is easy to see from (5.1) that ∂t(ukN,vkN)=0\partial_{t}(u_{k}^{N},v_{k}^{N})=0 for |k|>N|k|>N. Therefore (5.1) is effectively a finite system of ODEs.

The following proposition follows by standard arguments of ODE theory since the nonlinearity in cKdV is locally Lipschitz.

Proposition 5.1.

Let the initial data (u​i​n,v​i​n)∈(H˙0)2(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}. For every positive integer NN, there exists T>0T>0 such that problem (5.1) has a unique solution (uN​(t),vN​(t))∈(H˙0)2(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\in(\dot{H}^{0})^{2} on the time interval [0,T][0,T]. The solution can be extended to a maximal interval of existence [0,Tmax)[0,T_{\max}) such that either Tmax=+∞T_{\max}=+\infty, or if TmaxT_{\max} is finite then one has lim supt→Tmax−‖(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙0)2=+∞\limsup_{t\rightarrow T_{\max}^{-}}\left\|(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}=+\infty.

The next result shows that the solution (uN,vN)(u^{N},v^{N}) of the Galerkin system can not blow up in finite time in (H˙0)2(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}, and therefore Tmax=+∞T_{\max}=+\infty.

ℰ⁡(uN​(t),vN​(t)):=2​‖uN​(t)‖H˙02+2​‖vN​(t)‖H˙02+‖uN​(t)−vN​(t)‖H˙02\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t)):=2\left\|u^{N}(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}+2\left\|v^{N}(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}+\left\|u^{N}(t)-v^{N}(t)\right\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}^{2}

By Proposition 5.1, it is sufficient to show the conservation of ℰ⁡(uN​(t),vN​(t))\mathcal{E}(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t)) on the interval [0,Tmax)[0,T_{\max}). Thus, in the proof, we consider t∈[0,Tmax)t\in[0,T_{\max}). Let us rewrite the quantity ℰ⁡(uN​(t),vN​(t))\mathcal{E}(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t)) as

=∑0<|k|≤N6​∂tukN​u−kN+2​∂tvkN​v−kN−2​∂tukN​v−kN−2​∂tvkN​u−kN,\displaystyle=\sum_{0<|k|\leq N}6\partial_{t}u_{k}^{N}{u}^{N}_{-k}+2\partial_{t}v_{k}^{N}{v}_{-k}^{N}-2\partial_{t}u_{k}^{N}{v}^{N}_{-k}-2\partial_{t}v_{k}^{N}{u}^{N}_{-k}\>,

where we have used u¯kN=u−kN\overline{u}^{N}_{k}=u^{N}_{-k} and the fact ∂t(ukN,vkN)=0\partial_{t}(u_{k}^{N},v_{k}^{N})=0 for |k|>N|k|>N.

=:A.\displaystyle=:A\>. (5.4)

Now we address estimates for higher order Sobolev norms of the global solution of the Galerkin system (5.1). In order to do that we utilize the second form of the equation. Taking the solution (uN,vN)(u^{N},v^{N}) of our Galerkin system (5.1) we see that it satisfies the Galerkin version of the second form (4) of the cKdV introduced in Section 4, namely

∂t[(ukNvkN)−(B2N​(uN,vN)k−B2N​(uN,uN)kB2N​(uN,vN)k−B2N​(vN,vN)k)+𝐁3N​(uN,vN)k]\displaystyle\partial_{t}\left[\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u^{N}_{k}\\ v^{N}_{k}\end{array}\right)-\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}-B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},u^{N})_{k}\\ B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}-B_{2}^{N}(v^{N},v^{N})_{k}\end{array}\right)+\mathbf{B}_{3}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}\right]
=𝐑3resN​(uN,vN)k+𝐁4N​(uN,vN)k,k∈ℤ0,\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}+\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}\>,\quad k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\>, (5.10)

where we use the notations

B2N​(ϕ,ψ):=𝒫​B2​(𝒫​ϕ,𝒫​ψ),𝐁3N​(ϕ,ψ):=𝒫​𝐁3​(𝒫​ϕ,𝒫​ψ),\displaystyle B_{2}^{N}(\phi,\psi):=\mathcal{P}B_{2}(\mathcal{P}\phi,\mathcal{P}\psi)\>,\quad\mathbf{B}_{3}^{N}(\phi,\psi):=\mathcal{P}\mathbf{B}_{3}(\mathcal{P}\phi,\mathcal{P}\psi)\>,
𝐑3resN​(ϕ,ψ):=𝒫​𝐑3res​(𝒫​ϕ,𝒫​ψ),𝐁4N​(ϕ,ψ):=𝒫​𝐁4​(𝒫​ϕ,𝒫​ψ).\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N}(\phi,\psi):=\mathcal{P}\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}(\mathcal{P}\phi,\mathcal{P}\psi)\>,\quad\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N}(\phi,\psi):=\mathcal{P}\mathbf{B}_{4}(\mathcal{P}\phi,\mathcal{P}\psi)\>.

The next result states, for any T>0T>0, the high order Sobolev norms of the Galerkin system solutions (uN,vN)(u^{N},v^{N}) are bounded on [0,T][0,T] uniformly in NN.

Proposition 5.3.

Assume s≥0s\geq 0, (u​i​n,v​i​n)∈(H˙s)2(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}, and T>0T>0. Let (uN​(t),vN​(t))(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t)) be the solution of the Galerkin system (5.1) over the interval [0,T][0,T] with the initial data (u​i​n,v​i​n)(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}}). Then (uN​(t),vN​(t))(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t)) solves (5) and satisfies the estimate

‖(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙s)2≤C⁡(‖(u​i​n,v​i​n)‖(H˙0)2,T,s),for allt∈[0,T],\left\|(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq C\left(\left\|(u^{\emph{in}},v^{\emph{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}},T,s\right)\>,\quad\text{for all}\quad t\in[0,T]\>, (5.11)

where the bound is independent of NN.

Proof.

Due to the fact that we are dealing with a finite number of ODEs (and finite sums) we observe by straight forward calculation (differentiation by parts twice) as in Section 3 and Section 4 that a solution of  (5.1) also solves (5).

Throughout, we consider t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. By (5.1) (or (5)), it is clear that, ∂t(ukN,vkN)=0\partial_{t}(u_{k}^{N},v_{k}^{N})=0 for |k|>N|k|>N. Therefore,

‖(I−𝒫)​(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙s)2=‖(I−𝒫)​(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)2≤‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)2.\left\|(I-\mathcal{P})(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}=\left\|(I-\mathcal{P})(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\>. (5.12)

It follows that ‖(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙s)2\left\|(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}} is bounded for every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Our goal, however, is to show that the bound on the HsH^{s}-norm is uniform in NN.

In (5) we set

𝐳kN:=(ukNvkN)−(B2N​(uN,vN)k−B2N​(uN,uN)kB2N​(uN,vN)k−B2N​(vN,vN)k)+𝐁3N​(uN,vN)k,\mathbf{z}^{N}_{k}:=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u^{N}_{k}\\ v^{N}_{k}\end{array}\right)-\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}-B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},u^{N})_{k}\\ B_{2}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}-B_{2}^{N}(v^{N},v^{N})_{k}\end{array}\right)+\mathbf{B}_{3}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}, (5.13)

then (5) goes over to

∂t𝐳kN=𝐑3resN​(uN,vN)k+𝐁4N​(uN,vN)k,k∈ℤ0.\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{z}^{N}_{k}=\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k}+\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})_{k},\;\;k\in\mathbb{Z}_{0}\>. (5.14)

Since 𝐁4\mathbf{B}_{4} gives a maximal gain of ε<1/2\varepsilon<1/2 spatial derivatives according to (4.14), we fix a positive integer n0n_{0} such that s/n0=ε<1/2s/n_{0}=\varepsilon<1/2. Once we establish the uniform bound in (H˙ε)2(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}, we can iterate the argument and after n0n_{0} steps we will have the desired bound in (H˙s)2(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}.

Put M0:=‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙0)2M_{0}:=\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}. Due to the conservation law established in Proposition 5.2, one has

‖(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙0)2≤C⁡(M0), for all ​t∈[0,T].\displaystyle\left\|(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}\leq C(M_{0}),\text{\;\;for all\;\;}t\in[0,T]. (5.15)

Here C⁡(M0)C(M_{0}) is a constant depending on M0M_{0}, and it may change hereafter from line to line. It is clear that the mapping properties of 𝐑3resN\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N} and 𝐁4N\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N} are the same as the ones of 𝐑3res\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}} and 𝐁4\mathbf{B}_{4}, and thus by (4.4), (4.14) and (5.15), we obtain

‖𝐑3resN​(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2+‖𝐁4N​(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2≤C⁡(M0)​(‖(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2+1).\left\|\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+\left\|\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}\leq C(M_{0})\big(\left\|(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+1\big). (5.16)

Taking into account equation (5.13) and the smoothing properties of B2B_{2} and 𝐁3\mathbf{B}_{3} (see Lemma 8.2 and the estimate (4.13)), we have

‖(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2≤‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)2+C⁡(M0),\left\|(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}\leq\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+C(M_{0}), (5.17)

and therefore together with (5.16), one has

‖𝐑3resN​(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2+‖𝐁4N​(uN,vN)‖(H˙ε)2≤C⁡(M0)​(‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)2+1).\left\|\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+\left\|\mathbf{B}_{4}^{N}(u^{N},v^{N})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}\leq C(M_{0})(\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+1). (5.18)

Then, we see from (5.14) and (5.18) that

‖∂t𝐳N‖(H˙ε)2≤C⁡(M0)​(‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)2+1).\displaystyle\left\|\partial_{t}\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}\leq C(M_{0})(\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}+1). (5.19)

By (5.13) and the fact that ‖(uN​(t),vN​(t))‖(H˙s)2<∞\left\|(u^{N}(t),v^{N}(t))\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}<\infty for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], it is clear that ‖𝐳N​(t)‖(H˙s)2\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}} is also finite for every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Thus, we calculate

∂t‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)22=2​⟨∂t𝐳N,𝐳N⟩(H˙ε)2\displaystyle\partial_{t}\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}^{2}=2\left\langle\partial_{t}\mathbf{z}^{N},\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\rangle_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}} ≤‖∂t𝐳N‖(H˙ε)22+‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)22\displaystyle\leq\left\|\partial_{t}\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}^{2}+\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}^{2}
≤C⁡(M0)​(‖𝐳N‖(H˙ε)22+1),\displaystyle\leq C(M_{0})(\left\|\mathbf{z}^{N}\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{\varepsilon})^{2}}^{2}+1),

where (5.19) has been used. Then, by means of Gronwall’s inequality, we have

where the bound is uniform in NN. It is worth to mention that, the uniform bound above depends on the H˙0\dot{H}^{0}-norm, and not the H˙s\dot{H}^{s}-norm of the initial data. ∎

We now establish the existence of global solutions (without uniqueness) which is stated in Theorem 2.3 for the case s>0s>0. Also we show the conservation law (2.12) and the bound (2.11). The uniqueness and continuous dependence on initial data for s>0s>0 will be justified in Section 6 and 7. The case s=0s=0 will be treated in Section 7.

6. Uniqueness for s>1/2s>1/2

In the previous section we established global existence, without uniqueness, of solutions to the cKdV system (2.6) in the space (H˙s)2(\dot{H}^{s})^{2} for s>0s>0. Here, we will using the Banach Fixed Point Theorem to establish the uniqueness of solutions, as well as the continuous dependence on initial data for s>1/2s>1/2. The case s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2] will be treated in the next section.

In [1], where the periodic KdV was studied, the authors also used the contraction mapping argument to establish the uniqueness. However, their technique depends on the invertibility of a linear operator, which relies on the fact that one can solve a 1d-boundary value problem for an ODE explicitly and estimate its solution. But such method is infeasible to adopt here for our cKdV system, since the linearization of the left-hand side of (3) may not be invertible, where the difficulty lies in explicitly solving a boundary value problem for a system of two coupled ODEs in which the situation is much more complicated. In order to bypass this obstacle, we split solutions properly into high and low Fourier modes, and recast the differentiation by parts procedure to terms involving high frequencies for the sake of taking advantage of the time-averaging induced squeezing. Similar idea was also used in [1] to treat the so-called less regular initial data (0≤s≤1/20\leq s\leq 1/2), and in [10] (following [1]) to study the unconditional uniqueness of the modified KdV equation for s≥1/2s\geq 1/2. We believe that this kind of approach is more natural and general, especially for systems, which avoids studying the invertibility of a linear operator, so it is easier to implement to other dispersive equations for establishing uniqueness of solutions. In fact, one of the main purposes of this paper is to demonstrate this idea for such a typical system.

Let N≥1N\geq 1 be an integer that will be selected later. Recall, 𝒫\mathcal{P} defined in (5) denotes the projection on the low Fourier modes |k|≤N|k|\leq N. In addition, we define 𝒬=I−𝒫\mathcal{Q}=I-\mathcal{P}, where II is the identity map. Observe that 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} both depend on NN.

We decompose B1​(u,v)B_{1}(u,v) by splitting the Fourier modes of uu and vv into high and low modes. More precisely,

B1​(u,v)=B1​(𝒫​u,𝒫​v)+[B1​(𝒫​u,𝒬​v)+B1​(𝒬​u,v)].\displaystyle B_{1}(u,v)=B_{1}(\mathcal{P}u,\mathcal{P}v)+\left[B_{1}(\mathcal{P}u,\mathcal{Q}v)+B_{1}(\mathcal{Q}u,v)\right].

It can be shown, by elementary analysis, that any solution of the original cKdV (2.6) in the sense of Definition 2.1 also satisfies the integrated modified first form (6). Therefore, the uniqueness of solutions to (6) on [0,T∗][0,T^{*}] implies the uniqueness for (2.6) on [0,T∗][0,T^{*}]. By extension, the global solution constructed in Section 5 is the unique solution of (2.6), and it is in the space C⁡([0,T],(H˙s)2)C([0,T];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}), for any T>0T>0, and s>1/2s>1/2.

‖𝐁40​(u,v)−𝐁40​(u~,v~)‖(H˙s)2\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{B}_{40}(u,v)-\mathbf{B}_{40}(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}
≤C⁡(s)​‖(u,v)−(u~,v~)‖(H˙s)2​(‖(u,v)‖(H˙s)23+‖(u~,v~)‖(H˙s)23).\displaystyle\leq C(s)\left\|(u,v)-(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\left(\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}+\left\|(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}\right). (7.21)

By virtue of (7.1), (7.9) and (7.17), we can write 𝐑3Q​(u,v)\mathbf{R}_{3}^{Q}(u,v) as

𝐑3Q​(u,v)\displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{3}^{Q}(u,v) =𝐑3resQ​(u,v)+𝐑3nresQ​(u,v)\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres}}^{Q}(u,v)
=𝐑3resQ​(u,v)+𝐑3nres1Q​(u,v)+𝐑3nres0Q​(u,v)\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres1}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres0}}^{Q}(u,v)
=𝐑3resQ​(u,v)+𝐑3nres1Q​(u,v)+∂t𝐁30​(u,v)+𝐁40​(u,v).\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres1}}^{Q}(u,v)+\partial_{t}\mathbf{B}_{30}(u,v)+\mathbf{B}_{40}(u,v). (7.22)

Substituting (7.22) into the modified first form (6), we obtain the following modified second form of the cKdV:

∂t[(uv)−𝐁2Q​(u,v)−𝐁30​(u,v)]\displaystyle\partial_{t}\left[\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\right)-\mathbf{B}_{2}^{Q}(u,v)-\mathbf{B}_{30}(u,v)\right]
=𝐁1P​(u,v)+𝐑3resQ​(u,v)+𝐑3nres1Q​(u,v)+𝐁40​(u,v).\displaystyle=\mathbf{B}_{1}^{P}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres1}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{B}_{40}(u,v). (7.25)

We now use this form of the cKdV to prove the uniqueness of global solutions and continuous dependence on initial data in the space (H˙s)2(\dot{H}^{s})^{2} for s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2].

Proof.

The integrated form of (7) reads

(uv)​(t)−\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\right)(t)- (uv)​(0)=[𝐁2Q​(u,v)+𝐁30​(u,v)]​(t)−[𝐁2Q​(u,v)+𝐁30​(u,v)]​(0)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\right)(0)=\left[\mathbf{B}_{2}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{B}_{30}(u,v)\right](t)-\left[\mathbf{B}_{2}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{B}_{30}(u,v)\right](0)
+∫0t[𝐁1P(u,v)+𝐑3resQ(u,v)+𝐑3nres1Q(u,v)+𝐁40(u,v)](τ)dτ.\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t}\left[\mathbf{B}_{1}^{P}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres1}}^{Q}(u,v)+\mathbf{B}_{40}(u,v)\right](\tau)d\tau. (7.30)

Let (y⁡(t),z⁡(t)):=(u⁡(t),v⁡(t))−(uin,vin)(y(t),z(t)):=(u(t),v(t))-(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}}). Using the new variables yy and zz, (7) can be written as a fixed point equation

(y,z)=ℱ⁡(y,z)\displaystyle(y,z)=\mathscr{F}(y,z) (7.31)

where

ℱ\displaystyle\mathscr{F} (y,z)​(t)=𝐁2Q​(y⁡(t)+uin,z⁡(t)+vin)+𝐁30​(y⁡(t)+uin,z⁡(t)+vin)\displaystyle(y,z)(t)=\mathbf{B}_{2}^{Q}(y(t)+u^{\text{in}},z(t)+v^{\text{in}})+\mathbf{B}_{30}(y(t)+u^{\text{in}},z(t)+v^{\text{in}})
−𝐁2Q​(uin,vin)−𝐁30​(uin,vin)\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt-\mathbf{B}_{2}^{Q}(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})-\mathbf{B}_{30}(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})
+∫0t[𝐁1P(y(τ)+uin,z(τ)+vin)+𝐑3resQ(y(τ)+uin,z(τ)+vin)\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t}\Big[\mathbf{B}_{1}^{P}(y(\tau)+u^{\text{in}},z(\tau)+v^{\text{in}})+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3res}}^{Q}(y(\tau)+u^{\text{in}},z(\tau)+v^{\text{in}})
+𝐑3nres1Q(y(τ)+uin,z(τ)+vin)+𝐁40(y(τ)+uin,z(τ)+vin)]dτ.\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt+\mathbf{R}_{\text{3nres1}}^{Q}(y(\tau)+u^{\text{in}},z(\tau)+v^{\text{in}})+\mathbf{B}_{40}(y(\tau)+u^{\text{in}},z(\tau)+v^{\text{in}})\Big]d\tau. (7.32)

We intend to show ℱ\mathscr{F} maps the ball of radius AA, which is,

{(y,z)∈C0​([0,T∗],(H˙s)2):‖(y,z)‖C⁡([0,T∗],(H˙s)2)≤A},\displaystyle\{(y,z)\in C_{0}([0,T^{*}];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}):\left\|(y,z)\right\|_{C([0,T^{*}];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2})}\leq A\}, (7.33)

for s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2], into itself and is a contraction map provided that T∗T^{*} is sufficiently small. To see this, we let (y,z)(y,z) and (y~,z~)(\tilde{y},\tilde{z}) be in the ball (7.33). Then, due to the mapping properties (6.20), (6.21), (6.22), (6.23), (7.2), (7.3), (7.11), (7.12), (7.18), (7.19), (7.20), (7.21) and the definition (7.32) of ℱ\mathscr{F}, we deduce that, for s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2],

‖ℱ⁡(y,z)​(t)‖(H˙s)2≤C⁡(s)N​(A2+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)22)+γ⁡(N,s)​(A3+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)23)\displaystyle\left\|\mathscr{F}(y,z)(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq\frac{C(s)}{N}\left(A^{2}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{2}\right)+\gamma(N,s)\left(A^{3}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}\right)
+T∗[C(s,N)(A2+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)22)+C(A3+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)23)\displaystyle+T^{*}\Big[C(s,N)\left(A^{2}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{2}\right)+C\left(A^{3}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}\right)
+C(N,s)(A3+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)23)+C(s)(A4+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)24)].\displaystyle\hskip 28.90755pt+C(N,s)\left(A^{3}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}\right)+C(s)\left(A^{4}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{4}\right)\Big].

One observes that the left-hand side, i.e., ‖ℱ⁡(y,z)​(t)‖(H˙s)2\left\|\mathscr{F}(y,z)(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}} is independent of NN. In addition,

‖ℱ⁡(y,z)​(t)−ℱ⁡(y~,z~)​(t)‖(H˙s)2≤‖(y,z)​(t)−(y~,z~)​(t)‖(H˙s)2\displaystyle\left\|\mathscr{F}(y,z)(t)-\mathscr{F}(\tilde{y},\tilde{z})(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq\left\|(y,z)(t)-(\tilde{y},\tilde{z})(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}
×{C⁡(s)N(A+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)2)+γ(N,s)(A2+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)22)\displaystyle\times\Big\{\frac{C(s)}{N}\left(A+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\right)+\gamma(N,s)\left(A^{2}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{2}\right)
+T∗[C(s,N)(A+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)2)+C(A2+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)22)\displaystyle\hskip 14.45377pt+T^{*}\Big[C(s,N)\left(A+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\right)+C\left(A^{2}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{2}\right)
+C(N,s)(A2+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)22)+C(s)(A3+‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)23)]},\displaystyle\hskip 28.90755pt+C(N,s)\left(A^{2}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{2}\right)+C(s)\left(A^{3}+\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}^{3}\right)\Big]\Big\},

where γ⁡(N,s)→0\gamma(N,s)\rightarrow 0 as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. We observe once again that the left-hand side of the above inequality is independent of NN. Thus, for any A>0A>0, we can choose NN sufficiently large, and T∗T^{*} small enough, so that ‖ℱ⁡(y,z)​(t)‖(H˙s)2≤A\left\|\mathscr{F}(y,z)(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq A, ‖ℱ⁡(y~,z~)​(t)‖(H˙s)2≤A\left\|\mathscr{F}(\tilde{y},\tilde{z})(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq A, and

‖ℱ⁡(y,z)​(t)−ℱ⁡(y~,z~)​(t)‖(H˙s)2≤12​‖(y,z)​(t)−(y~,z~)​(t)‖(H˙s)2,\left\|\mathscr{F}(y,z)(t)-\mathscr{F}(\tilde{y},\tilde{z})(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|(y,z)(t)-(\tilde{y},\tilde{z})(t)\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}},

for all t∈[0,T∗]t\in[0,T^{*}], where T∗T^{*} depends on AA and ‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙s)2\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}}. By the Banach’s Fixed Point Theorem, there exists a unique solution (y,z)(y,z) of (7.31) on [0,T∗][0,T^{*}] in the ball (7.33), which yields the short-time existence and uniqueness of the solution (u,v)(u,v) to (7) in the space (H˙s)2(\dot{H}^{s})^{2} for s∈[0,1/2]s\in[0,1/2].

It can be shown that any solution of the original cKdV (2.6) in the sense of Definition 2.1 also satisfies the integrated modified second form (7). Also, recall in Section 5, we have already proved the global existence of solutions for the original cKdV (2.6) for s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2]. Therefore, according to the uniqueness result proved above and using some extension argument, we conclude that the global solution of (2.6) is unique, and it is in the space C⁡([0,T],(H˙s)2)C([0,T];(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}) for any T>0T>0, and s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2].

Finally, similar to the proof in Section 6, we can also show the continuous dependence on the initial data for the case s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2]. ∎

Remark 7.1.

Notice from the above that the contraction mapping argument is valid for s=0s=0. Hence, provided there is a solution of (2.6) for the case s=0s=0, we also obtain the uniqueness and continuous dependence on initial data for the equation (2.6) if s=0s=0.

It remains to show the existence of a solution to (2.6) for the case s=0s=0. This will be done by using density arguments.

Proof.

We approximate the initial data (uin,vin)∈(H˙0)2(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{0})^{2} by a sequence of smoother functions (ujin,vjin)∈(H˙s)2(u_{j}^{\text{in}},v_{j}^{\text{in}})\in(\dot{H}^{s})^{2}, where s>0s>0. Let us fix an arbitrary T>0T>0. We have already shown that, for each jj, there exists a unique solution (uj​(t),vj​(t))∈C⁡([0,T],(H˙0)2)(u_{j}(t),v_{j}(t))\in C([0,T];(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}) such that (uj​(0),vj​(0))=(ujin,vjin)(u_{j}(0),v_{j}(0))=(u_{j}^{\text{in}},v_{j}^{\text{in}}), and the quantity ℰ⁡(uj​(t),vj​(t))\mathcal{E}(u_{j}(t),v_{j}(t)), defined in (2.12), is conserved. By Remark 7.1, we infer

‖(uj,vj)−(uℓ,vℓ)‖L∞​([0,T],(H˙0)2)≤L​‖(ujin,vjin)−(uℓin,vℓin)‖(H˙0)2,\left\|(u_{j},v_{j})-(u_{\ell},v_{\ell})\right\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T],(\dot{H}^{0})^{2})}\leq L\left\|(u_{j}^{\text{in}},v_{j}^{\text{in}})-(u_{\ell}^{\text{in}},v_{\ell}^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}\>, (7.34)

where LL depends on TT and ‖(uin,vin)‖(H˙0)2\left\|(u^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})\right\|_{(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}}. Since (ujin,vjin)(u_{j}^{\text{in}},v_{j}^{\text{in}}) is a Cauchy sequence in (H˙0)2(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}, we deduce from (7.34) that (uj,vj)(u_{j},v_{j}) is a Cauchy sequence in C⁡([0,T],(H˙0)2)C([0,T];(\dot{H}^{0})^{2}), whereas we denote the limit as (u,v)(u,v). Now, using the mapping properties of B1B_{1}, one can pass to the limit in equation (2.9) similar as in Section 5 (where we proved the existence for s>0s>0), and deduce that (u,v)(u,v) also satisfies (2.9) and conserves ℰ⁡(u⁡(t),v⁡(t))\mathcal{E}(u(t),v(t)), defined in (2.12), for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Finally, by Remark 7.1 again, we obtain the desired uniqueness and continuous dependence on initial data under the (H˙0)2(\dot{H}^{0})^{2} norm. ∎

8. Appendix: relevant estimates

In this section we collect all relevant estimates for the nonlinear operators entering in our equations. The notations are not, or just slightly, different from the ones used in [1], where all proofs can be found.

Lemma 8.1.

Let θ>3/2\theta>3/2. Then the bilinear operator B1B_{1} defined in (2.8) maps H˙0×H˙0\dot{H}^{0}\times\dot{H}^{0} into H˙−θ\dot{H}^{-\theta} and satisfies the estimate

‖B1​(ϕ,ψ)‖H˙−θ≤C⁡(θ)​‖ϕ‖H˙0​‖ψ‖H˙0.\|B_{1}(\phi,\psi)\|_{\dot{H}^{-\theta}}\leq C(\theta)\|\phi\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}\|\psi\|_{\dot{H}^{0}}.

Let s>−1/2s>-1/2. Then the bilinear operator B2B_{2} defined in (3.11) maps H˙s×H˙s\dot{H}^{s}\times\dot{H}^{s} into H˙s+1\dot{H}^{s+1} and satisfies the estimate
